When OpenTelemetry is more than you need

Choose a monitoring tool by starting from the question you need answered. An OpenTelemetry pipeline means running a collector and a backend and making content decisions. It is worth that cost when you need per-user token counts, costs and tool activity, or traces of individual runs. Many questions need far less. Spend per workspace, how many developers used Claude Code this week, or what one agent session cost can each be answered with no collector at all.
The lightweight options are already built in. The Agent SDK message stream reports token and cost data your application can read directly. A Managed Agents session carries a
object with its token counts, active seconds and list cost. A

event delivers the same snapshot on the stream, so you don't need to poll. For an organization, the Usage & Cost API returns usage and cost by workspace, model and API key. For Claude Code on a Team or Enterprise plan, the analytics dashboard covers adoption.

Checkpoint 1 of 5
Check yourself

A platform team runs Claude Managed Agents. Finance wants to know what each individual agent session cost, updated as sessions finish. The team does not need per-user tool activity or traces. Which approach answers this with the least infrastructure?
Poll each session on a timer, because the API offers no way to push usage totals
Read the session's usage field, or listen for the session.usage event on the session stream, with no collector
Query the Usage & Cost API, because it breaks spend down by individual agent session
Deploy an OpenTelemetry collector and backend, set OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp, and add up the cost metrics per session

Attributing spend with the Usage & Cost API
The Usage & Cost API answers organization-level questions with an Admin API key and no infrastructure. It has two endpoints.
returns token counts in 1-minute, 1-hour or 1-day buckets.

The API's limits show when it is the wrong tool. Data usually appears within about five minutes of a request, and the API supports polling once per minute over sustained use. That suits dashboards and budget alerts, but not debugging live. It also has no concept of an individual user. The Console's usage and cost pages cannot break spend down by user, and issuing one API key per developer to fake it runs into performance limits. For per-user Claude Code costs, use the Claude Code Analytics API instead.

An analyst wants hourly dollar figures per workspace from the cost endpoint to catch a spend spike within the day. What will they find?
The cost endpoint returns daily buckets only, so intraday detail has to come from token counts in the usage endpoint
The cost endpoint has no time buckets and returns a single total for the date range
The cost endpoint accepts 1m, 1h and 1d buckets, the same as the usage endpoint
The cost endpoint returns hourly buckets only when grouped by workspace_id

Per-user attribution on Bedrock, Agent Platform and Foundry
Predict first
A team runs Claude Code through Google Cloud's Agent Platform and wants per-developer spend in an Anthropic-hosted view. Which one works?
Neither: the cloud provider's traffic needs OpenTelemetry or a gateway
A Console workspace spend limit on a linked workspace
The Claude for Enterprise analytics dashboard, once an admin enables it

Where Claude Code is billed decides which monitoring tools can see it. Each Anthropic-hosted view covers only its own billing channel. The org analytics spend report covers usage-credit spend on Team and Enterprise plans. Console workspace spend limits govern Console API usage.

opens claude.ai or organization usage settings, or sends a request to your admins. When requests go to Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, none of these sees the traffic.

OpenTelemetry or an LLM gateway

On these providers, the right tool depends on whether you need caps or only visibility. OpenTelemetry exported from each machine gives per-user token counts, costs and tool activity whatever the provider, but it can only report a cap, not enforce one. To split those figures by developer and team, set
, the variable that attaches your own key=value tags, such as

, to the metric datapoints Claude Code exports. The value is comma-separated pairs with no spaces. A self-hosted Claude apps gateway placed in front of the provider adds per-user usage attribution, OTLP token metrics and per-user spend limits it enforces. When a developer passes their cap, the gateway blocks their requests until the period resets. A generic LLM gateway such as LiteLLM tracks spend per key. It is unaffiliated with Anthropic and has not had a security audit.
Exam trap
Once an admin enables it, the analytics dashboard or Console workspace limits also cover Claude Code traffic sent through Amazon Bedrock.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 3 of 5
Check yourself

Your developers' Claude Code requests are billed through Amazon Bedrock. Finance wants token and cost figures broken down by developer and team. They don't need to block anyone yet. Which tool gives them this?
OpenTelemetry metrics exported from each developer machine, tagged with user and team keys in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES
The analytics spend report for the Claude organization, once an admin links the Bedrock account
The AWS billing console, because it already shows all of the Bedrock spend for Claude
Console workspace spend limits, with one workspace for each team
Checkpoint 4 of 5
Exam question

A company runs Claude Code through Amazon Bedrock and notices that, unlike their Claude Console workspace, no per-developer cost or token metrics appear in any Anthropic-hosted dashboard. Finance still wants per-user spend attribution and enforceable per-user caps. What should the platform team deploy to get this?
A self-hosted Claude apps gateway in front of Bedrock, which adds per-user usage attribution, OTLP token metrics, and per-user spend limits that Bedrock itself does not send to Anthropic
The Claude for Enterprise analytics dashboard at claude.ai/analytics/claude-code, which aggregates Bedrock spend the same way it aggregates Console spend once an admin enables it
The /usage-credits command run on each developer's machine, which sets an organization-wide monthly spend limit that automatically covers the entire Bedrock deployment
The workspace spend limit feature in the Claude Console, applied to the Bedrock-linked workspace, since Console workspace limits are documented to govern usage across all providers uniformly

Sizing TPM and RPM allocations by organization size

Rate limits are set at the organization level, so a Claude Code rollout needs one total allocation, not a set of individual ones. To size it, multiply the headcount by the per-user tokens-per-minute (TPM) and requests-per-minute (RPM) figures for your team-size tier. The per-user figure falls steeply as the team grows, so a figure taken from a small pilot overstates what a large organization needs per developer.

Here is a worked case. A 15-developer pilot sits in the 5–20 tier at 100k–150k TPM per user. Scaling to 300 developers with that figure gives 30M–45M TPM. The 100–500 row is the correct one for 300 developers: 15k–20k TPM and 0.37–0.47 RPM per user, or roughly 4.5M–6M TPM and 111–141 RPM in total. Once usage comes from Console accounts, Claude Code gets its own workspace with its own usage and rate limits, separate from your other workloads. Workspace limits can be set lower than the organization's limits, but not higher.
Exam trap
The per-user TPM measured in a small pilot can be multiplied by the full headcount to size the organization's allocation.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 5 of 5
Exam question

An organization is scaling its Claude Code rollout from 15 developers to roughly 300 developers and wants to set organization-level Tokens-Per-Minute and Requests-Per-Minute allocations. A junior admin proposes simply multiplying the 15-user TPM-per-user figure by 300. Why is this the wrong approach, and what should the admin do instead?
Per-user TPM/RPM shrinks as org size grows since fewer users are concurrently active at scale, so the admin should multiply by the lower per-user figure for the 300-user tier, not the 15-user figure

Per-user TPM/RPM recommendations stay flat regardless of organization size, so the admin's multiplication using the 15-user figure is already correct and no further adjustment is needed before rollout
Rate limits are enforced per individual user rather than at the organization level, so aggregate TPM/RPM planning is unnecessary once each developer already has their own individual allocation set
TPM/RPM sizing only matters for Bedrock and Vertex deployments, so an organization authenticating through the Claude Console can safely ignore these per-user figures during its rollout planning
